fields.Frequency: Occasional (estimated 2–5 closures/relocations per year as network matures to 300+ stores)
fields.Participants: COO, VP Store Operations, Real Estate (Property Mgmt Inc.), IT, Finance, HR, Supply Chain, Marketing
fields.Trigger: Persistent underperformance, lease expiry non-renewal, market exit, or relocation to better site
fields.Volume: 1 store at a time; each takes 2–3 months from decision to final close-out

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-review of "review triggers closure decision" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System rule-based auto-approval of "CEO and Board approve closure/relocation" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-generate of "generates transfer orders from closing store to nearest stores and serving DC" (replaces manual Step 4).
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)
- operational: VP Store Operations review and approval gate; operational: periodic reconciliation against source documents
Pain Points / Risks: - Employee morale and attrition cascade — announcing closure triggers immediate productivity drop and voluntary resignations from high performers before redeployment can be arranged, leaving the store understaffed during wind-down
- Inventory write-down risk — aggressive redistribution timelines may force markdowns or discounts to move slow-moving inventory quickly, eroding recovery value
- LGU permit retirement delays — failure to retire the business permit within 30 days results in continued local business tax billing; Philippine LGU bureaucracy can delay closure acknowledgment
- Customer loyalty attrition — even with proactive reassignment to nearest store, ~20–30% of closing store's loyalty members become inactive within 6 months of closure
Staffing Implication: - **VP Store Operations**: Leads closure process. ~20 hours per closure spread over 2–3 months.
- **Supply Planner**: Mass redistribution planning adds ~1 week per closure. Absorbed within existing team.
- **HR**: Up to 30 separations + redeployments per closure. Absorbed within existing HR team with advance planning.
- **IT**: 1 week per store decommission. 2–3 IT staff per closure. With 2–5 closures/year, this is ~5–15 staff-weeks. Absorbed within existing IT team.
- **Finance**: Final P&L close-out adds ~1 day per closure. Absorbed.
System Touchpoints: - Mass transfer order generation from closing store to multiple destinations (W45.4)
- Store location deactivation: status change, transaction blocking, removal from active reporting (W45.12)
- Employee redeployment (transfer between locations in same entity) vs. separation processing per W43 (W45.6)
- Fixed asset disposal trigger for store-specific assets per W39 (W45.11)
- Customer account reassignment to new default store (W45.7)
- Trade/AR account collection and reassignment (W45.8–9)
- Final store financial close-out with closure P&L recognition (W45.13)
- Closed location data retention with restricted access (W45.14)

- Financial close-out checklist: petty cash return, gift card/store credit reissuance, special order deposit refund or fulfillment, warranty claim reassignment, backorder release, vendor contract termination per W62, final service invoice verification (W45.13a)
- LGU permit retirement: closure notification to LGU BPLO, final LBT payment, LGU closure acknowledgment, location master update (W45.13b)

- Integration with W25 (petty cash return), W28 (gift card reissuance), W33 (warranty reassignment), W38 (special order deposit refund), W54 (LGU permit retirement), W56 (backorder release), W62 (vendor contract termination)
Time Estimate: 2–3 months total cycle per closure. Key effort concentrations: VP Store Operations ~20 hours over 2–3 months, Supply Planner ~1 week for redistribution plan, HR ~2–4 weeks for redeployment/separation of up to 30 staff, IT ~1 week for decommission, Finance ~1 day for final P&L. Financial close-out checklist (W45.13a) requires 1 full day of combined Controller/Store Manager effort.

steps.activity: Store performance review triggers closure decision: sustained negative EBITDA, declining foot traffic, lease renewal at unfavorable terms, or strategic market exit
CEO and Board approve closure/relocation; VP Store Operations appointed as closure lead
Property Mgr Inc. negotiates lease termination with landlord; settles any penalties or early termination fees
Supply Planner creates mass inventory redistribution plan: system generates transfer orders from closing store to nearest stores and serving DC; prioritizes by item velocity and destination need
DC and receiving stores process inbound transfers per standard receiving (W22, W3); closing store picks and ships inventory in waves over 1–2 weeks

HR initiates employee action: (a) redeploy high-performers to nearby stores (transfer, not separation), (b) offer voluntary separation to others, (c) process separations per W43 for staff not redeployed; peak: up to 29 separations per store (the full §12.1 store headcount)

Marketing executes customer communication plan: notify loyalty members of closure, redirect to nearest store, offer relocation promotion (e.g., extra loyalty points at new nearest store), update store locator on website/app
Customer Service handles inbound inquiries from trade/corporate accounts; reassigns accounts to nearest store's Sales Rep or Regional Manager
AR Clerk reviews and collects any outstanding trade/corporate account balances specific to closing store location
IT decommissions store infrastructure: POS terminals, network equipment, RF devices (reverse of W16.3); deactivates store location in ERP system; removes from price file and replenishment routing
Cost Accountant disposes store fixtures and fixed assets per W39 (disposal/retirement); capitalizes any leasehold improvement write-offs
System deactivates store location master: location status set to "Closed"; no further transactions posted; location excluded from reports and dashboards
Controller runs final store P&L and balance sheet reconciliation: all inventory cleared, all AP/AR settled, all assets disposed; final profit/loss on closure recognized

**Financial close-out checklist** — Controller and Store Manager verify the following location-specific commitments are resolved before final close: (a) petty cash float (PHP 20K) returned to Treasury via bank transfer or armored car; custodian reconciliation completed per W25; (b) gift cards / store credit vouchers issued by closing store — system reissuance to customer's nearest store location with customer notification; unredeemed store credit balance recognized as revenue upon closure; (c) pending special orders (W38) — customer deposits either fulfilled from alternative store/DC or refunded per W38.16 deposit refund process; (d) pending warranty claims (W33) — items at vendor for repair reassigned to customer's nearest store for pickup upon return; (e) pending backorders (W56) — allocation released or redirected to nearest store with customer notification; (f) store-specific vendor contracts (e.g., local maintenance, cleaning) — terminated per W62 with final payment; (g) store-specific service contracts — final invoice verified and paid; (h) **loyalty profile default-store reassignment**: system identifies all loyalty members whose registered default store is the closing store; system automatically reassigns each member's default store to the nearest active BuildRight store based on geographic proximity; affected members notified via SMS/email with new default store information; loyalty points, tier status, and transaction history unaffected by reassignment
steps.r: Controller / Store Manager / AR Clerk / AP Clerk

steps.activity: **LGU permit retirement**: Regulatory Officer notifies LGU Business Permit and Licensing Office (BPLO) of store closure; files closure notification with final local business tax payment (covering period up to closure date); obtains LGU closure acknowledgment; system updates location master with closure date and LGU retirement confirmation per W54; failure to retire LGU permit may result in continued LBT billing — Regulatory Officer confirms retirement within 30 days of closure
Post-closure: system retains closed store data for 10-year retention period (BIR); historical data accessible for reporting but location excluded from active operations

fields.Trigger: Employee wishes to purchase merchandise for personal use

workflows.name: Employee Purchase Program & Internal Staff Sales

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-validate of "verifies active employment status and “Monthly Purchase Limit”" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-apply of "applies “Staff Discount”" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-review of "reviews high-frequency staff purchases for potential abuse" (replaces manual Step 5).
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)
- operational: Store Manager / HR Manager review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - Resale abuse — employees purchasing items at staff discount for resale to third parties (friends, sari-sari stores, online marketplace) at profit, violating the "personal use only" policy and eroding margin on discounted items
- Manager sign-off bypass — Store Managers rubber-stamping employee purchase receipts without verifying items are for personal use, especially during busy periods when the 1-min sign-off is rushed

- Payroll deduction disputes — employees disputing salary deductions for purchases they claim were unauthorized or for different amounts than expected; resolution requires cross-referencing POS transaction logs with payroll records

- Policy inconsistency across stores — different Store Managers applying different interpretations of what constitutes "personal use" (e.g., purchasing materials for a family member's home renovation), creating fairness complaints and potential HR grievances
Staffing Implication: - ~1,000 transactions/month chain-wide (per the Frequency) ÷ 200 stores ≈ 0.2/store/day × ~5 min ≈ ~1 min/store/day of POS time (~80 hours/month chain-wide). Absorbed by existing Cashiers.
- Store Manager sign-off: ~1 min per transaction. LP monthly audit: 2–4 hours chain-wide. No incremental headcount.
- HR handles payroll deduction disputes as part of standard HR operations — estimated 5–10 disputes/month chain-wide.
System Touchpoints: - POS Employee Purchase tender type with employee ID verification and active employment status check via HR integration (W205.1)
- Automated staff discount application with configurable category-level rules (cost + 5% or 15% off SRP) (W205.2)
- Monthly purchase limit enforcement per employee (e.g., PHP 20,000/month) with running total tracking (W205.1)
- Payroll deduction integration for employee purchases via salary deduction (W10/W76) (W205.3)
- LP audit dashboard for high-frequency and high-value employee purchase pattern detection (W37) (W205.5)
- Integration with W5B (POS selling — employee purchase workflow), W10 (payroll — salary deduction), W37 (loss prevention — abuse detection), VS-19 HRIS (employee records master)
Time Estimate: ~5 min per employee purchase transaction (1 min eligibility check + 2 min payment + 1 min manager sign-off + 1 min receipt). At ~1,000 transactions/month across 6,762+ employees, total POS time is ~80 hours/month. LP monthly audit: 2–4 hours. HR eligibility verification is automated.

steps.activity: **Eligibility Check**: Employee presents ID at POS; System verifies active employment status and "Monthly Purchase Limit" (e.g., PHP 20,000/month)
**Discount Application**: System applies "Staff Discount" (e.g., Cost + 5% or 15% off SRP) based on product category rules
**Payment**: Employee pays via Cash, Card, or "Payroll Deduction" (W10/W76)
**Verification**: Manager signs receipt; confirms items are for personal use (not resale)
**Audit**: LP Team reviews high-frequency staff purchases for potential abuse (W37)

fields.Participants: Store Manager, Department Supervisors, employees, HR Coordinator (HQ)
fields.Trigger: Start of store business day; ongoing throughout operating hours

workflows.name: Store-Level Daily HR Operations & People Management

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-review of "reviews daily attendance report from biometric/RFID system" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-flag of "For unplanned absences" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-record of "record and payroll input" (replaces manual Step 3).
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)
- operational: backup RFID badge scanning; operational: real-time overtime budget tracking in Step 4
Pain Points / Risks: - **Attendance system downtime**: biometric failure requires manual punch entry with supervisor confirmation per W561; mitigated by backup RFID badge scanning
- **Overtime budget overruns**: store-level overtime exceeding monthly allocation triggers Regional Manager review; mitigated by real-time overtime budget tracking in Step 4
- **Inconsistent leave approval**: Store Managers may apply leave policies inconsistently across 200 stores; mitigated by system-enforced policy rules and Regional Manager audit
- **Employee relations sensitivity**: Store Managers may lack HR training for employee relations issues; mitigated by HR Coordinator hotline and escalation protocol to HR Business Partner
Staffing Implication: - **Store Manager**: ~30 min/day on HR operations (attendance, leave, overtime) + ~15 min/week on schedule review = ~3.5 hours/week. Absorbed within existing role.
- **Department Supervisors**: ~5 min/day on overtime requests and attendance follow-up = ~30 min/week per supervisor. Absorbed within existing role.
- **HR Coordinator (HQ)**: ~2 hours/week reviewing store-level HR reports and handling escalations from 200 stores. Absorbed within existing role.
System Touchpoints: - ERP HR module: attendance integration, leave management, overtime tracking, shift scheduling
- Biometric/RFID system: real-time attendance feed
- Mobile app: Store Manager HR dashboard, employee self-service for leave/swap requests
- Payroll module: daily payroll input accumulation
Time Estimate: ~28–31 min per store-day (attendance review 10 min + absence follow-up 5 min + same-day leave approvals 3 min each + overtime authorization 5 min + shift-swap handling 5 min; employee check-ins 5 min each as needed) ≈ 170–190 hours/store/year ≈ 34,000–38,000 hours/year chain-wide, plus the Friday coverage-gap review 15 min ≈ 13 hours/store/year (daily HR summary automated).

steps.activity: Store Manager reviews daily attendance report from biometric/RFID system; identifies absences, late arrivals, and missing punches

For unplanned absences: Department Supervisor contacts employee to determine reason (sick leave, emergency, AWOL); system auto-flags "absent without notification" if no contact by 1 hour after shift start
Leave approval for same-day requests: Store Manager approves/denies based on department coverage; emergency leave auto-approved per policy; system updates attendance record and payroll input

Overtime authorization: Department Supervisor submits overtime request with business justification (unexpected customer traffic, delivery backlog, inventory count); Store Manager approves/denies; system tracks overtime budget utilization vs. monthly allocation per W602

Shift swap requests: Employee A initiates swap with Employee B (same skill set); both confirm; Department Supervisor verifies coverage; Store Manager approves; system updates schedule and attendance rules

Employee relations quick-check: Store Manager conducts brief check-in with any employee flagged for attendance issues, performance concerns (per W72), or personal matters affecting work; documents outcome
System generates daily HR summary: attendance rate, overtime hours, leave usage, open HR action items; auto-submits to Regional Manager HR dashboard
Weekly (Fridays): Store Manager reviews upcoming week schedule for coverage gaps; submits schedule change requests to HR Coordinator; confirms weekend staffing adequacy

fields.Frequency: Daily monitoring; weekly review; semi-monthly reconciliation
fields.Participants: Store Manager, Department Supervisors, Regional Manager, HR Coordinator, Finance Analyst
fields.Trigger: Start of pay period (semi-monthly); weekly review trigger

workflows.name: Store-Level Labor Cost Monitoring & Overtime Budget Control

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-calculate of "calculates daily labor cost flash" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-review of "reviews daily labor cost as % of daily revenue on morning dashboard" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-log of "If amber/red alert" (replaces manual Step 3).
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)
- operational: tracking absolute hours vs; operational: automated holiday calendar in payroll module per HR-011; operational: system requirement for same-day overtime entry in W601
Pain Points / Risks: - **Revenue volatility distorts labor cost %**: stores with revenue dips (weather, local events) show elevated labor cost % even with controlled hours; mitigated by tracking absolute hours vs. budget in addition to percentage

- **Philippine holiday complexity**: with 12 regular holidays and 9 special non-working days, holiday premium calculations are complex and error-prone; mitigated by automated holiday calendar in payroll module per HR-011
- **Delayed overtime data**: if overtime approvals are not entered same-day, labor cost flash is inaccurate; mitigated by system requirement for same-day overtime entry in W601
Staffing Implication: - **Store Manager**: ~20 min/day on labor cost review + ~15 min/week on weekly review + ~30 min semi-monthly reconciliation = ~3 hours/week. Absorbed within existing role.
- **Finance Analyst**: ~2 hours semi-monthly on consolidation + ~4 hours/quarter on budget review. Absorbed within existing FP&A role.
System Touchpoints: - ERP HR/Payroll module: hours worked, overtime, premium calculations, budget allocation
- ERP Finance module: labor cost GL posting, budget vs. actual reporting
- BI dashboard: store-level labor cost flash, trend analysis, ranking
Time Estimate: Daily per-store cycle 5–15 min (labor-cost flash review 5 min + overtime-log review 10 min on amber/red alerts) ≈ 6,100–18,250 hours/year chain-wide; weekly review and overtime forecast 25 min/store ≈ 4,300 hours/year; semi-monthly payroll-vs-budget reconciliation 30 min/store ≈ 2,400 hours/year; Finance consolidation of the 200-store flash 2 hours per cycle and quarterly budget review 4 hours — total ≈ 12,800–25,000 hours/year (per the itemized daily/weekly/semi-monthly components; daily flash calculation automated).

steps.activity: System calculates daily labor cost flash: total regular hours × hourly rate + overtime hours × premium rate + holiday premium (if applicable) + night differential; compares to daily budget allocation
Store Manager reviews daily labor cost as % of daily revenue on morning dashboard; target: labor cost ≤ 12% of store revenue; amber alert at > 14%; red alert at > 16%

If amber/red alert: Store Manager reviews overtime authorization log (per W601 Step 4) and identifies departments exceeding allocation; implements corrective action (reduce remaining week overtime, adjust schedules)
Weekly (Monday): Store Manager reviews prior week labor cost report with breakdown by department, overtime category (customer-driven vs. operational), and trend vs. prior 4 weeks
Department Supervisors submit overtime forecast for upcoming week with business justification; Store Manager approves aggregate overtime budget allocation per department
Semi-monthly: Store Manager reconciles actual payroll (from W10) vs. store labor budget; investigates variances > 5%; submits variance explanation to Regional Manager and Finance Analyst
Finance Analyst consolidates 200-store labor cost flash report for CFO review; identifies top/bottom 10 stores by labor cost %; flags chronic over-budget stores for remediation
Quarterly: Finance and HR review store-level labor budgets against actual; adjust allocation formulas based on store revenue, format size, and seasonal patterns

fields.Frequency: As needed; estimated ~80–120 incidents/month across 200 stores
fields.Participants: Store Manager, Department Supervisor, employee, HR Coordinator (HQ), HR Business Partner, witness(es)
fields.Trigger: Employee policy violation, attendance infraction, performance issue, misconduct, or customer complaint against employee

workflows.name: Store-Level Employee Disciplinary Process & DOLE Due Process Compliance

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-record of "Incident occurs or is reported" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-log of "logs if POS-related" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-document of "documents verbal warning in system with date, nature, and improvement…" (replaces manual Step 4).
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)

- operational: system-enforced workflow with mandatory NTE issuance before NOD; operational: NTE issuance before NOD; operational: policy matrix with offense severity classification and HR Coordinator review in Steps 5 and 7
Pain Points / Risks: - **DOLE due process non-compliance**: failure to follow two-notice rule (NTE → NOD) or denial of opportunity to explain results in illegal dismissal finding; mitigated by system-enforced workflow with mandatory NTE issuance before NOD
- **Inconsistent discipline across stores**: Store Managers may apply different standards; mitigated by policy matrix with offense severity classification and HR Coordinator review in Steps 5 and 7

- **Retaliation claims**: employees may claim disciplinary action was retaliatory for union activity or whistleblower reports (W79); mitigated by HR Business Partner independent review for termination cases
- **Witness cooperation**: witnesses may be reluctant to provide statements against coworkers; mitigated by confidential reporting option and anti-retaliation policy
Staffing Implication: - **Store Manager**: ~30 min per incident (investigation + documentation); ~10–15 hours/month across all incidents. Absorbed within existing role.
- **HR Coordinator**: ~30 min per incident for compliance review; ~5 hours/month. Absorbed within existing role.
- **HR Business Partner**: ~1 hour per termination case; ~4–6 hours/month for severe offense reviews. Absorbed within existing role.
System Touchpoints: - ERP HR module: disciplinary case management, employee master data, warning tracking
- Document management: NTE/NOD template generation and storage (W255)
- CCTV system: footage retrieval for investigation (per W207)
- POS transaction logs: evidence for POS-related incidents (per W522)
Time Estimate: ~1.1–2.5 hours per incident depending on severity (documentation 10 min + fact-finding 30 min + classification 5 min + one disposition path — verbal counseling 15 min, written warning 30 min, or termination-track review 60 min + explanation review 15 min + Notice of Decision 30 min + preventive-suspension handling 15 min where applied); at ~80–120 incidents/month chain-wide ≈ 1,000–1,500 incidents/year ≈ 1,050–3,600 hours/year, plus the monthly disciplinary summary 2 hours (employee-master recording automated).

steps.activity: Incident occurs or is reported: Department Supervisor or Store Manager documents initial observation with date, time, location, nature of incident, witnesses; system creates disciplinary case record
Store Manager conducts preliminary fact-finding: interviews employee, witnesses, reviews CCTV footage (per W207), reviews system transaction logs if POS-related

Store Manager classifies offense severity per policy matrix: Minor (tardiness, dress code, minor policy violation), Moderate (insubordination, repeated minor offenses, customer service failure), Severe (theft, fraud, violence, safety violation, gross misconduct)

**For Minor offenses — Verbal Warning**: Store Manager conducts private counseling with employee; documents verbal warning in system with date, nature, and improvement expectation; system tracks verbal warning count (3 verbal warnings = 1 written warning)

**For Moderate offenses or repeated Minor — Written Warning**: Store Manager drafts written notice of explanation (NTE) per DOLE two-notice rule; employee given 5 business days to submit written explanation; NTE references specific company policy violated and incident details
Employee submits written explanation or waives right to respond; Store Manager and HR Coordinator evaluate explanation; if explanation is unsatisfactory, proceed to Step 7

**Notice of Decision (NOD)**: Store Manager issues written decision with disciplinary action: written warning, suspension (1-30 days per severity), or termination recommendation for severe offenses; HR Coordinator reviews for DOLE compliance before issuance

**For Severe offenses — Preventive Suspension**: If investigation requires more than 5 days, employee placed on preventive suspension (max 30 days per Labor Code) with pay; Store Manager coordinates with HR Business Partner for investigation

**For termination cases**: HR Business Partner conducts independent review; ensures two-notice rule compliance, just cause per Article 297 Labor Code, and due process documentation; Legal Counsel reviews if employee is regular status; final termination decision by VP Legal & Compliance
All disciplinary actions recorded in employee master (W292) with immutable audit trail; system flags employees with active disciplinary actions for promotion/transfer eligibility check

Monthly: HR Coordinator generates store-level disciplinary summary report; Regional Manager reviews for pattern analysis (specific stores with high incident rates may indicate management or training issues)

fields.Frequency: As needed; ~1,200–1,600 new hires/year across 200 stores (~6–8 per store per year per profile §11.4)
fields.Participants: New employee, assigned Buddy (experienced Sales Associate), Department Supervisor, Store Manager
fields.Trigger: New hire first day at store (following HQ onboarding per W15)
fields.Volume: 1 new hire per event; ~100–130 active buddy assignments at any time (~30-day window on ~1,200–1,600 hires/year)

workflows.name: Store-Level New Employee Buddy System & First-Week Onboarding

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-validate of "checks Buddy eligibility and current assignment load" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-identify of "identify knowledge gaps" (replaces manual Step 5).
- System auto-review of "reviews and adds comments" (replaces manual Step 6).
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)

- operational: mandatory Buddy training module and Store Manager selection oversight; operational: Buddy training module and Store Manager selection oversight; operational: assigning backup Buddy and cross-training multiple eligible buddies per department
Pain Points / Risks: - **Buddy quality inconsistency**: not all experienced employees make good trainers; mitigated by mandatory Buddy training module and Store Manager selection oversight

- **Buddy absenteeism**: if Buddy is absent during first week, new hire loses critical orientation time; mitigated by assigning backup Buddy and cross-training multiple eligible buddies per department
- **First-week overwhelm**: too much information in first 3 days leads to poor retention; mitigated by structured Day 1-5 progression with specific daily objectives
- **High early turnover**: new hires who leave within 90 days waste buddy investment; mitigated by realistic job preview during recruitment (W15) and first-week engagement check
Staffing Implication: - **Buddy (Sales Associate)**: ~8 hours Week 1 (full shift shadowing) + ~2 hours/week Weeks 2-4 = ~16 hours total per new hire. Absorbed within existing role with schedule accommodation.
- **Department Supervisor**: ~30 min Week 1 + ~15 min/week Weeks 2-4 = ~1.5 hours per new hire. Absorbed within existing role.
- **Store Manager**: ~20 min Week 1 setup + ~10 min end-of-week review + ~20 min 30-day review = ~50 min per new hire. Absorbed within existing role.
System Touchpoints: - ERP HR module: buddy assignment tracking, assessment forms, onboarding milestone completion
- Employee master (W292): buddy eligibility flag, current assignment status, onboarding status
- Mobile app: buddy assessment form, check-in reminders, progress dashboard
- BI module: buddy program effectiveness analytics, retention correlation
Time Estimate: ~4 hours of direct buddy/manager effort per new hire (buddy assignment 10 min + Day-1 tour 1 hour + department orientation 2 hours + check-ins and assessments ~45 min across weeks 1–4 + 30-day review 20 min); days-2–3 shadowing runs within regular shifts; at ~1,200–1,600 new hires/year ≈ 4,800–6,400 hours/year chain-wide (program metrics automated).

steps.activity: Prior to new hire arrival: Store Manager assigns Buddy from same department — selection criteria: ≥ 6 months tenure, performance rating ≥ satisfactory, completed Buddy training module; system checks Buddy eligibility and current assignment load (max 1 buddy at a time)

**Day 1**: Buddy meets new hire at store entrance; provides store tour (selling floor, backroom, break room, emergency exits, first aid station, restrooms); introduces to all team members by name and role

Buddy guides new hire through department-specific orientation: product locations, top 20 selling SKUs, shelf layout, price tag reading, safety hazards specific to department (heavy items in lumber, chemicals in paint, sharp tools in hardware)

**Days 2-3**: Buddy shadows and is shadowed — new hire observes Buddy handling customer interactions, POS transactions (if cashier), and department tasks; Buddy explains reasoning and shares tips; new hire attempts first customer interactions with Buddy present

**Days 4-5**: New hire handles customer interactions independently with Buddy available for questions; Department Supervisor conducts 15-minute check-in to assess comfort level and identify knowledge gaps

**End of Week 1**: Buddy completes first-week assessment form: new hire's product knowledge (top 20 SKUs), customer interaction confidence, POS familiarity, safety awareness, areas needing improvement; Department Supervisor reviews and adds comments
Store Manager reviews first-week assessment; schedules additional training for identified gaps; if performance is below expectations, extends buddy period by 1 week with specific improvement targets

**Weeks 2-4**: Buddy check-ins reduce to twice weekly; Department Supervisor conducts weekly progress assessment; by Week 4, new hire should meet basic competency thresholds per W518 (if cashier) or department standards

**End of Month 1**: Store Manager conducts formal 30-day review; if competency thresholds met, buddy assignment formally ends; if not met, remediation plan created with HR Coordinator; system updates employee record with onboarding completion status

System tracks buddy program metrics per store: average onboarding duration, 30-day competency pass rate, 90-day retention rate for buddy-supported hires vs. non-buddy; monthly report to HR Coordinator

fields.Participants: Vendor Promodizer, Department Supervisor, Store Manager, HR (promodizer compliance per W269)
fields.Trigger: Vendor promodizer arrives at store for scheduled or unscheduled floor activity; or daily promodizer schedule review
fields.Volume: ~2–5 promodizers active per store during promo periods; ~12,000–30,000 promodizer check-ins/month chain-wide (daily per the staffing cadence)

workflows.name: Store-Level Vendor Promodizer Floor Activity Coordination & Compliance

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-review of "Daily promodizer schedule review" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-validate of "check-in" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-assign of "assigned area only" (replaces manual Step 3).
Background: Vendor promodizers (merchandiser demonstrators, product promoters, and brand ambassadors deployed by vendors to BuildRight stores) are a common feature of Philippine big-box retail. With ~800–1,000 vendors, many deploy promodizers to maintain shelf presence, conduct product demonstrations, and influence purchase decisions. W269 covers enterprise-level promodizer management and W449 covers DOLE 174 labor compliance. This workflow addresses the daily store-level coordination challenge: managing multiple promodizers from different vendors operating simultaneously on the sales floor, ensuring they follow BuildRight rules, and preventing conflicts between promodizer activities and store operations.
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)
- operational: strict check-in process and requirement for advance scheduling; operational: clear vendor control of promodizer tasks and W449 compliance monitoring
Pain Points / Risks: - **Unscheduled promodizer visits**: vendors frequently send promodizers without prior scheduling, disrupting store operations and creating coverage conflicts; mitigated by strict check-in process and requirement for advance scheduling

- **Promodizer boundary violations**: promodizers may overstep their authorized area, approaching customers in departments they are not assigned to, or making unauthorized claims about competing products

- **DOLE 174 compliance risk**: if BuildRight is deemed to be directing promodizer work activities (rather than the vendor), DOLE may classify promodizers as BuildRight employees, triggering benefits obligations; mitigated by clear vendor control of promodizer tasks and W449 compliance monitoring
- **Customer disturbance**: aggressive promodizers who follow customers, use loud speakers, or create congestion can degrade the shopping experience and generate customer complaints per W41
Staffing Implication: Department Supervisors: ~20–30 min/day per store on promodizer coordination (10-15 min schedule review + 5 min × 2-5 check-ins + 5 min × 2-5 check-outs). Absorbed within existing Department Supervisor duties. No incremental headcount.
System Touchpoints: - Promodizer scheduling module integrated with W269 vendor promodizer management
- Visitor badge/floor access system linked to W581 vendor representative access
- Activity logging and compliance tracking
- Incident reporting integration per W471
- Vendor communication module per W269 for feedback routing
- POS promotional setup per W523 for demo-related pricing
Time Estimate: **Total per store per day**: 20-30 min (schedule review 10-15 min + check-in 5 min/promodizer + monitoring 5-10 min/check + check-out 5 min/promodizer). Chain-wide: ~67–100 hours/day.

steps.activity: **Daily promodizer schedule review**: Store Manager or Department Supervisor reviews daily promodizer schedule: (a) system displays scheduled promodizer visits: vendor name, promodizer name, assigned department, approved activity (demonstration, shelf stocking, product sampling, inventory check), approved time window; (b) identify conflicts: multiple promodizers in same department, overlapping demo stations, promodizer scheduled during peak traffic when floor space is limited; (c) resolve conflicts by adjusting time slots or relocating activity areas

**Promodizer check-in**: upon arrival: (a) promodizer reports to customer service counter or department supervisor; (b) Department Supervisor verifies: (i) promodizer has valid BuildRight-issued ID/visitor badge per W581 vendor access management; (ii) promodizer is on the approved schedule; (iii) activity type matches approved activity for today; (c) if unscheduled visit: Store Manager decides to allow (if space available and activity is pre-approved type) or decline (redirect to vendor's BuildRight account manager for scheduling); (d) issue floor access badge with time-limited validity

**Floor activity monitoring**: during promodizer activity: (a) Department Supervisor periodically checks promodizer activity (every 1-2 hours): (i) promodizer is in assigned area only; (ii) not interfering with customer shopping flow; (iii) not disparaging competing products; (iv) following BuildRight store rules: no loud music, no blocking aisles, no unauthorized promotional materials; (v) wearing required PPE if in paint/chemical department per W237; (b) if violations observed: (i) first offense: verbal warning and correction; (ii) repeated offense: ask promodizer to leave and report to vendor via W269; (iii) serious violation (customer harassment, theft, safety hazard): immediate removal and incident report per W471

**Product demonstration coordination**: for promodizers conducting live product demonstrations: (a) Department Supervisor assigns demonstration area: not blocking main aisles, near relevant product section, with access to power outlet if needed; (b) verify demonstration materials are safe: no open flames, no hazardous chemicals without PPE, no food samples without sanitary compliance; (c) ensure demonstration does not create excessive noise or waste; (d) coordinate with cashier team if promodizer is offering special pricing or coupons that need POS setup per W523

**Promodizer check-out**: at end of activity: (a) promodizer returns floor access badge; (b) Department Supervisor conducts brief debrief: (i) activity completed as planned?; (ii) any incidents or customer complaints?; (iii) any store property damage?; (iv) any inventory discrepancies noted?; (c) Department Supervisor logs visit completion in system with activity notes; (d) feedback sent to vendor via W269 promodizer management for performance tracking

fields.Participants: All on-shift store associates, Department Supervisors, Store Manager
fields.Trigger: Store opening preparation (scheduled daily, 15 minutes before store opens)

workflows.name: Store-Level Daily Huddle & Morning Team Briefing

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-review of "reviews overnight system alerts" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-issue of "issues from W608" (replaces manual Step 3).
- System auto-schedule of "Today's priorities — Daily sales target, active promotions" (replaces manual Step 4).
Background: Each BuildRight Depot store conducts a 10–15 minute morning team briefing before store opening. This daily alignment ritual ensures all associates are informed of daily sales targets, active promotions, staffing assignments, safety reminders, and policy updates. For a 200-store chain, consistent daily communication is critical for operational execution, promotional compliance, and employee engagement.
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)
- operational: Store Manager review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - Inconsistent briefing quality across 200 stores — without a structured template, some Store Managers may skip critical elements, leading to uneven execution
- Time pressure before store opening may cause rushed or skipped huddles, especially during peak seasons (Ber months)
- Part-time or late-shift associates miss morning huddle entirely, creating information gaps for afternoon/evening operations
- No mechanism to verify briefing compliance and content coverage across the chain
Staffing Implication: No incremental headcount. The huddle is conducted by the Store Manager as part of opening duties. 200 stores × 15 min/day = ~50 staff-hours/day across the chain, absorbed within existing Store Manager responsibilities.
System Touchpoints: - W665 store KPI dashboard — daily target and prior-day performance data
- W34 shift scheduling module — attendance verification against roster
- W13 promotional calendar — active promos for the day
- W571 communication module — overnight memos and directives
- W554 replenishment task list — incoming stock priorities
- W544 service order queue — scheduled installations/visits
Time Estimate: 10–15 minutes per store per day. Store Manager preparation: 5 minutes. Total daily time investment per store: 15–20 minutes.

steps.activity: Pre-huddle preparation — Store Manager reviews overnight system alerts (low-stock alerts from W554, LP overnight alerts from W562, memo inbox from W571), pulls daily targets from W665 KPI dashboard, and identifies key talking points
Team assembly — All on-shift associates gather at designated briefing area; Store Manager confirms attendance against shift roster (W34)
Yesterday's performance flash — Store Manager shares prior-day sales vs. target, top-performing departments, conversion rate, and any customer service highlights or issues from W608
Today's priorities — Daily sales target, active promotions (W13), planogram changes (W573), incoming deliveries (W18/W18B), scheduled services (W544), and special events (W147)
Safety minute — Quick safety reminder (topic rotates weekly: forklift safety, ladder safety, hazmat handling, fire safety, customer slip prevention) per W655 training schedule
Policy update & memo acknowledgment — Any new policy directives, product recalls (W29), price changes (W40), or urgent communications from W716
Staffing & assignment confirmation — Confirm department coverage, break schedules per DOLE requirements (W753), special assignments (inventory count zones, promo setup, vendor demos W745)
Team dispersal to stations — Associates proceed to assigned stations; opening procedures per W5A begin

fields.Frequency: Weekly collection per store; daily accumulation
fields.Participants: Maintenance/Utility Staff, Scrap Metal Collector (accredited buyer), Finance Analyst (revenue recognition)
fields.Trigger: Accumulation of scrap metal, cardboard, and recyclable materials from store operations
fields.Volume: ~100–200 kg scrap metal/store/week; ~300–500 kg cardboard/store/week; ~50–100 kg plastic/store/week

workflows.name: Store-Level Scrap Metal & Recyclable Material Collection & Revenue Recognition

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-record of "Weekly Collection & Weighing" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-review of "Revenue Recording & Cash Handling" (replaces manual Step 3).
- System auto-generate of "Quarterly Recycling Metrics & ESG Reporting" (replaces manual Step 4).
Background: BuildRight Depot's 200 stores generate significant recyclable waste from daily operations: damaged lumber (off-cuts, broken boards), scrap metal (damaged fixtures, wire offcuts, hardware returns), cardboard packaging (from inbound shipments), and plastic packaging. Philippine recycling infrastructure has matured significantly — accredited junk shops and scrap metal collectors (locally called "bote dyaryo" or "scrap buyers") serve every commercial area and pay market rates for sorted recyclable materials. Current market rates (2026): clean cardboard ~PHP 3–5/kg, scrap steel ~PHP 10–15/kg, scrap copper ~PHP 250–350/kg, aluminum ~PHP 50–70/kg, clean plastic ~PHP 5–8/kg. For a store generating 400–800 kg/week of recyclable material, this represents ~PHP 2,500–6,500/week (≈ PHP 10,000–27,000/month) in potential revenue per store (per the itemized rates and volumes) that is currently lost to improper disposal or untracked collection. Chain-wide, this represents ~PHP 22–65M/year in recyclable material value. Beyond revenue, proper recycling supports BuildRight's ESG commitments per W192 (GHG Emissions Tracking) and W193 (Waste Management & Circular Economy), reduces waste disposal costs per W502, and provides verifiable data for DENR waste diversion reporting per W433.
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)
- operational: Department Supervisor review and approval gate; operational: periodic reconciliation against source documents
Pain Points / Risks: - **Theft risk**: Scrap metal (especially copper and aluminum) has high street value and is a common theft target; scrap bins must be in secured receiving dock area (not accessible to customers); collector access logged per W581 (Vendor Representative Access); CCTV coverage per W838

- **Accreditation integrity**: Scrap collector must be DENR-accredited per W82 and properly registered as BuildRight vendor per W36; unaccredited collectors may illegally dump materials or resell to unregistered smelters; Finance team should verify collector accreditation annually

- **Revenue accuracy**: Manual weighing creates opportunity for under-weighing (collector benefit) or over-reporting (staff collusion); calibrated scale with digital readout and CCTV at weighing point per W838 mitigates risk; Department Supervisor must co-sign all weigh tickets

- **PFRS revenue recognition**: Scrap revenue is peripheral to BuildRight's core retail business; PFRS 15 requires recognition when collection occurs and payment is received; revenue should be immaterial to financial statements but must be properly recorded for tax compliance (BIR requires declaration of all income)
Staffing Implication: - **Maintenance Staff**: Weekly collection adds ~30–45 min/week; absorbed by existing Maintenance/Utility Staff
- **Department Supervisor**: Revenue recording and quarterly reporting adds ~15–20 min/week + 30–60 min/quarter
- **No incremental headcount**
System Touchpoints: - Waste tracking module with material category and weight logging
- Vendor master for accredited scrap collectors (W36)
- Cash handling and revenue recognition module (W541, W714)
- Store P&L reporting (W67, W489)
- ESG data collection module (W192, W694)
- Waste diversion rate analytics dashboard
- DENR waste reporting integration (W433)
Time Estimate: - Daily segregation: 5–10 min/day per staff (absorbed into workflow)
- **Total per store per week**: ~45–70 min dedicated time

steps.activity: **Daily Recyclable Material Segregation**: During daily operations: (a) Sales Associates and Receiving Clerks segregate waste into designated bins: (i) cardboard bin (flattened boxes, no food contamination), (ii) scrap metal bin (steel, copper, aluminum separated), (iii) plastic bin (clean packaging plastic, no chemical residue), (iv) wood/lumber bin (off-cuts, damaged boards — clean, no paint/treatment), (v) general waste bin (non-recyclable, per W502); (b) bins located at receiving dock and backroom; (c) hazardous materials (paint cans, solvent containers, chemical packaging) never placed in recycling bins — handled per W82 and W236

**Weekly Collection & Weighing**: Weekly: (a) accredited scrap collector arrives at scheduled time (registered vendor in ERP per W36); (b) Maintenance Staff and collector weigh each category of recyclable material using calibrated scale at receiving dock; (c) collector issues weigh ticket per category with unit price and total amount; (d) Maintenance Staff verifies weigh ticket accuracy and signs receipt; (e) collector pays cash or issues check per agreed terms; (f) system records collection: material category, weight (kg), unit price, total revenue, collector vendor code

**Revenue Recording & Cash Handling**: (a) cash received from scrap collector: counted by Maintenance Staff in presence of Department Supervisor; (b) cash deposited in store safe per W541 (Cash Office Operations); (c) system records revenue: debit cash, credit "Other Income — Scrap/Recycling Revenue" per GL account mapping; (d) revenue recognized in period collected per PFRS (realized revenue from recyclable sales); (e) if collector pays by check: check deposited per W89 (Bank Reconciliation) and W764 (Daily Opening Safe Count); (f) monthly scrap revenue reported in store P&L per W67 (Store Performance Review) and W489 (Store Operating Budget)

**Quarterly Recycling Metrics & ESG Reporting**: Quarterly: (a) system aggregates recycling data: total weight by material category per store per region; (b) total revenue from recycling per store; (c) waste diversion rate = total recycled weight ÷ total waste generated; (d) carbon offset estimate: recycled cardboard saves ~3.5 kg CO2/kg, recycled steel saves ~1.5 kg CO2/kg per DENR conversion factors; (e) metrics included in ESG data collection per W694 (ESG Data Collection & Annual Report Preparation); (f) Store Manager reviews recycling performance in quarterly store performance review per W67; (g) stores with waste diversion rate < 30% flagged for improvement action plan

fields.Frequency: Weekly × ~10–15 district managers (200 stores ÷ ~15 stores per district)
fields.Participants: Store Managers (15 per district), LP Officer, HR Business Partner, Finance Analyst
fields.Trigger: Weekly scheduled review (every Monday); also triggered by significant operational incident
fields.Volume: 15 stores per district manager per week

workflows.name: Multi-Store District Manager Weekly Operations Review & Compliance Audit

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-review of "Monday Morning District Dashboard Review" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-capture of "Store Visit & Structured Audit" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-document of "document coaching notes in system for follow-up tracking" (replaces manual Step 3).
Background: BuildRight Depot's 200 stores are organized into ~13–15 geographic districts (each district covers 13–15 stores within a 50–100 km radius), each led by a District Manager (DM) who reports to the COO via the Store Operations leadership. The DM is the critical management layer between HQ strategy and store-level execution. Each DM is responsible for: store revenue performance, operational compliance (planogram, pricing, cash handling, safety), customer experience scores, labor cost control, shrinkage reduction, and new store ramp-up. Without a structured weekly review cadence, DMs rely on ad-hoc store visits and reactive problem-solving, leading to inconsistent execution across the 200-store network. This workflow defines the DM's weekly review rhythm: Monday morning headquarters review with BI dashboards, Tuesday–Thursday store visits (2–3 stores/day with structured audit checklist), and Friday follow-up and reporting. The DM's weekly review ensures that all 200 stores are inspected at least once every 2–3 weeks (per the 6–9 visits/week district cadence), providing real-time field intelligence to HQ. This workflow is distinct from W67 (Monthly Store Performance Review) which is the store manager's self-review, and W575 (Store-Level Weekly Sales & Operations Review) which is the store's internal team meeting.
Controls: - CTL-262 (ensure controlled execution — Store Staffing & People (PA-07.4).)
- operational: District Manager (Regional Operations Manager) review and approval gate; operational: periodic reconciliation against source documents
Pain Points / Risks: - **DM workload balance**: Each DM covers 13–15 stores; visiting all stores weekly is impossible; the 5–6 week visit cycle means some problems fester between visits; BI dashboard (step 1) provides continuous visibility but cannot replace physical inspection; priority visit selection (step 1g) is critical

- **Audit fatigue**: Store Managers who receive frequent audit visits may develop resentment; DM must balance audit (compliance focus) with coaching (support focus); ratio should be 60% coaching, 40% audit; build rapport through recognition, not just criticism

- **Geographic coverage**: Districts covering island geography (e.g., Visayas district with stores on Cebu, Iloilo, and Bacolod) require air/sea travel between stores; DM may need 1–2 travel days per week, reducing available store visit time; consider sub-district structure for island districts

- **Data latency**: BI dashboard data may be 24–48 hours old by Monday morning; real-time POS data streaming per W533 reduces latency but not all KPIs update in real-time; DM should cross-reference dashboard data with in-store observations
Staffing Implication: - **District Manager**: 13–15 DMs covering 200 stores; each DM requires ~50–60 hours/week during peak periods; this is a senior operations role requiring strong analytical and coaching skills
- **LP Officer**: 1 LP Officer per district (13–15 total) supporting DM on loss prevention follow-up; partially shared with HQ LP team per W837
- **Finance Analyst**: 1 Finance Analyst per 2–3 districts supporting DM with financial analysis and budget review; shared with HQ Finance
- **Total incremental headcount**: 13–15 DMs + 13–15 LP Officers (already included in HQ headcount of 20 Regional LP Officers per model company profile)
System Touchpoints: - BI district dashboard with store-level KPI drill-down (W879, W665)
- Store audit checklist application (tablet-based) with barcode scanning for price checks
- Planogram compliance verification module (W573, W86)
- Pricing accuracy module (W667) with scan verification
- Cash management dashboard (W764, W541, W958)
- LP exception reporting (W837) with DM access for district-level view
- Store visit documentation system with coaching notes and action item tracking
- HR workforce management dashboard (W602, W594)
- Capital request system (W21) with DM submission capability
- Competitive intelligence module (W403) for field observations
Time Estimate: - Store visits (3 days × 2–3 stores × 90–120 min): 9–18 hours
- Coaching sessions: 45–60 min total per day

steps.activity: **Monday Morning District Dashboard Review**: DM reviews BI dashboard for all 15 stores in district: (a) **Sales performance**: week-over-week revenue, ATV, units per transaction, sales vs. budget, sales per sqm; red-flag stores > 10% below budget for 2+ consecutive weeks; (b) **Inventory health**: stockout rate by category, overstock alerts, replenishment order fill rate from DC, shrinkage trend; (c) **Customer experience**: customer satisfaction score (daily pulse from W608), NPS trend, complaint count and resolution time per W597; (d) **Labor**: overtime hours, labor cost as % of sales, attendance rate, unfilled positions; (e) **Cash & financial**: cash variance per W958, petty cash balance, bank deposit timeliness per W541; (f) **Compliance**: planogram compliance score (W573), price accuracy (W667), safety incident count (W140); (g) DM identifies 2–3 stores requiring priority visit this week based on performance outliers

**Store Visit & Structured Audit (2–3 stores/day, Tue–Thu)**: DM visits selected stores with standardized audit checklist on tablet: (a) **Store exterior**: parking lot cleanliness, signage condition, cart corral (W1028), garden center appearance (W722), security lighting; (b) **Store entrance**: welcome experience, promotional signage per W262, loyalty program visibility, basket/cart availability; (c) **Selling floor**: planogram compliance (check 3 random aisles per W573), shelf stock level (identify 5 empty shelf positions), pricing accuracy (scan 10 random items per W667), promotional display execution per W262, cleanliness and aisle obstruction; (d) **Backroom**: receiving area organization, damaged goods quarantine area (W91), hazmat storage compliance (W236), cycle count documentation (W6); (e) **Customer service counter**: BOPIS staging area (W11), return processing compliance (W12), queue management; (f) **Cash office**: safe count vs. system per W764, deposit preparation per W541, POS reconciliation documentation; (g) **Safety**: fire extinguisher inspection tags (W758), emergency exit clearance, PPE compliance in lumber yard; (h) **People**: observe 2–3 employee-customer interactions, check staff scheduling board, discuss any HR issues with Store Manager

**Store Manager Coaching & Action Plan**: During store visit, DM conducts 15–20 minute coaching session with Store Manager: (a) review Store Manager's weekly self-assessment per W575; (b) discuss top 3 performance gaps identified in dashboard and audit; (c) agree on 2–3 specific action items with deadlines (typically 1–2 weeks); (d) for high-performing stores: recognize achievements, capture best practices for sharing across district; (e) for underperforming stores: develop improvement plan with weekly checkpoints; (f) for new stores (< 6 months old): accelerated coaching per W702 (New Store Opening) milestones; (g) document coaching notes in system for follow-up tracking

**LP & Compliance Follow-Up**: DM reviews loss prevention exceptions with LP Officer: (a) exception-based reporting alerts per W837: high-risk transactions, void/refund patterns, cash handling anomalies; (b) CCTV incident review per W838: any flagged events requiring investigation; (c) shrinkage investigation status: open cases per W845 and resolution timeline; (d) compliance issues from audit: pricing errors, planogram violations, safety deficiencies; (e) DM and LP Officer agree on corrective actions and escalation for serious issues (theft investigation per W839, fraud per W841)

**Friday Summary Report & HQ Communication**: DM compiles weekly district summary: (a) district sales performance: total revenue, vs. budget, vs. last year, top 3 and bottom 3 stores; (b) audit findings summary: common issues across stores, systemic problems requiring HQ intervention; (c) action items from store visits with status (new/in-progress/completed); (d) resource requests: staffing (W555), capital (W21), maintenance (W47), or vendor issues; (e) competitive intelligence: any competitor activity observed during store visits (new store opening, aggressive pricing per W329); (f) submit report to COO via standardized template; (g) participate in weekly DM conference call with COO and other DMs (30 min): share cross-district learnings, escalate systemic issues, align on priorities
